title: Oregon QB Dante Moore Out for Season After Concussion, NBC Sports Reports
body:
Oregon’s once‑heralded quarterback Dante Moore will miss the remainder of the 2026 college football season after doctors confirmed that lingering concussion symptoms make a return unsafe. The decision, announced by head coach Dan Lanning on Monday, ends any chance for the senior signal‑caller to showcase his talents before the 2027 NFL Draft, a setback that reverberates through a program already grappling with an injury‑plagued roster.

Moore, who entered the year ranked among the top quarterback prospects for the upcoming draft class, suffered a hard‑hit concussion during Oregon’s week‑four matchup against Washington State. Although he was cleared to practice later in the month, he continued to experience headaches, sensitivity to light, and difficulty concentrating—symptoms that persisted despite a cautious rehabilitation protocol. After a comprehensive evaluation by the university’s sports‑medicine staff and an independent neurologist, the consensus was that further play would jeopardize his long‑term health and potentially diminish his draft stock.

The loss of Moore is a significant blow to the Ducks, who have struggled to find consistency at the position since the departure of former starter Bo Nix. In his three starts this season, Moore posted a 5‑2 record, threw for 1,842 yards, 14 touchdowns and three interceptions, and demonstrated a poise that had many analysts projecting him as a first‑round pick. Coach Lanning, who took over the program last year, praised Moore’s leadership and work ethic, noting that the quarterback “has been the heart of this offense, and his absence will be felt on and off the field.” The Ducks will now rely on junior backup Jake “J‑Train” Ramirez, a dual‑threat player with limited starting experience, to steer the offense through the final stretch of the Pac‑12 schedule.

The broader implications extend beyond Oregon’s immediate fortunes. Moore’s situation underscores the growing scrutiny surrounding concussion protocols in college football, a sport that has intensified its focus on player safety after a series of high‑profile incidents in recent years. The NCAA’s latest guidelines, adopted in 2024, require a multi‑step clearance process that includes neurocognitive testing, symptom monitoring, and a graduated return‑to‑play plan. Yet Moore’s case illustrates the challenges of balancing competitive pressure with medical caution, especially for athletes whose future professional prospects hinge on a single season of performance.

From a draft‑prospect perspective, Moore’s absence will likely shift his evaluation timeline. While his pre‑injury tape remains impressive, scouts will now have limited recent film to assess his development and durability. Draft analysts predict that Moore could still be selected in the early second round, provided he demonstrates a full recovery at the NFL Scouting Combine and maintains his physical conditioning during the off‑season. However, teams may approach him with heightened caution, possibly offering contracts with performance‑based incentives rather than the guaranteed money typically afforded to first‑round talent.

Looking ahead, Oregon’s coaching staff faces a dual challenge: keeping the team competitive in the final games and ensuring Moore’s health is fully restored before the next season. Lanning has indicated that the program will prioritize a “player‑first” philosophy, allowing Moore to focus on academic responsibilities and a structured rehabilitation regimen that includes cognitive therapy and gradual physical conditioning. The Ducks’ season now pivots on the development of their younger quarterbacks and the ability of the defense to compensate for any offensive shortfall.

As the Ducks prepare for their upcoming clash with rival Stanford, the narrative will shift from a quarterback‑centric offense to a test of depth, resilience, and strategic adaptability. For Dante Moore, the priority is clear: a complete recovery that safeguards his long‑term wellbeing and preserves his NFL aspirations. The coming months will determine whether the talent that once made him a draft darling can return to the field stronger, or whether this season will serve as a cautionary tale about the hidden costs of the sport’s relentless pace.
